cues.text: Chapter three: Replication and consistency.
Let's begin with the core idea.
Replication simply means creating copies of data.
There are choices in how you do it.
With full replication, every selected site stores all of the data.
With partial replication, only certain data is copied to each site.
Next, who is allowed to accept writes?
In leader-follower replication, all writes are directed to one leader, and the leader then copies the changes to its followers.
In multi-leader replication, writes are permitted at several leaders, and that comes with a cost: conflicts, because two leaders may accept different changes to the same data.
And in leaderless designs, the data lives on a set of replicas, and the system relies on coordination between them, and on read repair, to keep them in line.
Now, when does a write count as successful?
In synchronous replication, the system waits for the required acknowledgement before reporting success.
Depending on the protocol, this can improve durability and consistency.
In asynchronous replication, the system acknowledges the write before the remote copies have caught up.
That lowers latency, but it creates replication lag, and it can mean potential data loss at failover, because a copy that never received the update may become the new primary.
And one warning to remember: replication is not backup.
If someone deletes data, or data becomes corrupted, that deletion or corruption can be replicated too.
Let's turn to consistency, and be careful with the terms.
Strong consistency, as used in CAP, refers to linearizability.
That means operations behave as if each one takes effect atomically, in real-time order.
Eventual consistency means that replicas will converge, provided updates cease and communication resumes.
Notice that it does not bound staleness, so it tells you nothing about how long a stale value may persist.
Causal consistency preserves cause-and-effect ordering.
Two useful session guarantees are read-your-writes and monotonic reads.
And sequential consistency preserves each process's own order of operations, but it need not respect real-time order.
Here is an example.
In Lagos, a patient's address is updated.
In Enugu, someone reads that address before replication has caught up.
Under eventual consistency, an old value is permitted for a while.
Under linearizable access, the read would not return a value older than a completed write.
The practical lesson: clinical dosage decisions or payment decisions may need stronger guarantees than something like a cached directory.
Finally, quorums.
Suppose there are N replicas, a read quorum of size R, and a write quorum of size W.
Take N equals 3, R equals 2, and W equals 2.
Then R plus W is 4, which is greater than N, so the read quorum and write quorum must intersect; a read will always touch at least one replica that took the latest write.
Also, if W is greater than N divided by two, then write quorums intersect with each other as well.
Here, W equals 2 is greater than 1.5, so that holds.
But be careful: intersection alone does not guarantee linearizability.
Versioning, failure handling, and protocol design all matter.
Sloppy quorums can weaken the guarantees further.
And last, leader election and consensus protocols, such as Raft and Paxos, coordinate replicated state.
They are not the same thing as replication itself.
